routes.description: Establish that religious belief better secures moral knowledge and social judgment by grounding durable duties in divine authority and by showing that religious traditions can identify grave public evils more reliably than secular institutions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if divine authorship is given an adequate basis, transcendent authority explains the stability of binding duties, and the practical record supports religion's comparative capacity to recognize evil and sustain a good society.

motionBridge.description: Show that divine authority provides a firmer basis for moral knowledge and recognition of social evil than secular ethical deliberation provides.

centralBridges.description: Provide grounds for believing in an intentional creator and for treating sacred teaching as a credible source of moral authority.
Explain why divine authority makes core prohibitions binding and durable despite fallible human preferences and disagreement.
Show that a worldview's moral adequacy is tested by its capacity to identify major evils and contribute to a good society.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how disputed ancient rules may represent moral advances when interpreted within their historical setting.
Support the comparative claim that religious communities can recognize ideologically motivated evil that secular institutions overlook.

routes.description: Establish that secular ethical realism can guide moral knowledge and progress through evidence about conscious experience, rational inquiry, cooperation, and revisable public reasoning without relying on supernatural authorship or sacred authority.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if wellbeing and suffering furnish defensible moral facts, rational inquiry explains moral convergence and correction, and religious dogma is shown to be unnecessary or obstructive in identifying and remedying social evil.

motionBridge.description: Show that secular ethical realism can ground moral knowledge and moral progress without supernatural premises or sacred texts.

centralBridges.description: Ground moral distinctions in facts about the happiness, suffering, capacities, and relationships of conscious creatures.
Explain how open-ended rational inquiry can discover, test, and revise moral rules while distinguishing evidence-based realism from pragmatism.
Show how unsupported supernatural or political dogmas can motivate violence and obstruct effective moral judgment.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how attachment, reciprocity, mutual care, and viable social cooperation support prohibitions such as the rule against murder.
Show how secular analysis can make morally relevant distinctions among forms and stages of conscious life.

sections.title: Moral Authority and Binding Obligation
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether durable moral duties require divine command or can arise from rationally accessible facts about persons, cooperation, harm, and flourishing.

sections.title: Moral Knowledge and Ethical Realism
sections.rationale: The competing burdens require an account of how moral claims become knowable, objective, corrigible, and distinguishable from preference or mere practical success.

sections.title: Creator, Scripture, and Dogmatic Authority
sections.rationale: The status of a creator and sacred texts matters because the pro route invokes them as foundations while the con route challenges their evidentiary basis and moral reliability.

sections.title: Recognizing Social Evil and Testing Worldviews
sections.rationale: The debate uses communism, fascism, religious extremism, and institutional judgment to test which framework better identifies dangerous ideologies and supports moral progress.

sections.title: Consciousness, Human Status, and Contested Cases
sections.rationale: Disputes involving human uniqueness, animals, embryos, fetuses, suffering, and development test how each framework draws and justifies morally significant boundaries.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Claims that sacred books were written or informed by a supernatural creator are unsupported and dangerously divisive, particularly because they obstruct rational responses to religious extremism.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager directly invites Harris to characterize his view, and Harris delivers the ensuing first-person explanation without attribution ambiguity.

response.rationale: This is a constructive challenge to supernatural authorship and scriptural authority, so no earlier opposing locked move is targeted.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states a central evidentiary objection and connects it to practical harm.

precisionFindings.rationale: The objection is recoverable, but claims about being the most divisive dogma and paying a terrible price are broad and insufficiently bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The excerpt strongly declares supernatural authorship unsupported and exceptionally dangerous without supplying comparative support for the latter claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Unsupported supernatural authorship can coherently undermine scriptural authority, but the bridge from lack of support to exceptional divisiveness remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt identifies religious extremism as a consequence but offers assertion rather than representative evidence or comparison of rival causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central-tier attacks, it directly challenges the required credibility of creator-informed sacred teaching.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move directly advances its own evidentiary and practical claims rather than interpreting a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris calls supernatural authorship an ultimately unsupportable dogma and associates it with divisiveness and costs involving the Muslim world.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: Religious Americans are more likely than secular academics to recognize the threat of Islamic totalitarianism, supporting a comparative claim that religiosity can sharpen rather than impede the identification of grave social evil.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager explicitly speaks in the first person, identifies himself among religious Americans, and develops the challenge addressed to Harris.

components.text: Whether religion obstructs rational recognition of religious extremism.
Whether supernatural-scripture claims themselves are evidentially supported.
Whether such dogma is exceptionally divisive and dangerous overall.

response.rationale: Prager contacts the practical-obstruction component by claiming religious Americans recognize Islamic totalitarianism better, but does not answer supernatural authorship or the broader danger claim.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts a decisive practical component directly but leaves the foundational evidentiary challenge untouched.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison is clear, but categories such as religious Americans, evangelical leaders, and secular academics shift, and the claimed likelihood lacks boundaries.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A strong comparative frequency claim is asserted without sampling, base rates, or qualification concerning which religious and academic populations are compared.

charity.alternative: Harris can oppose supernatural dogma while conceding that some religious observers recognize Islamist threats accurately.
charity.decisiveQualification: That concession would not establish that religiosity generally improves recognition of social evil.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample coherently pressures a claim of obstruction, but recognition by selected religious leaders does not establish a general causal advantage for religiosity.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move relies on an attributed concession and an unverified group comparison without representative evidence or alternative causal analysis.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within subsidiary support, it directly advances religious discernment of ideologically motivated evil, though only through one contested comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: Prager identifies a genuine tension in the practical claim, though he overextends a bounded concession into a broad comparative conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager says evangelical Christian leaders are more likely than secular professors to acknowledge the threat from Islamic totalitarianism.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: When martyrdom, jihad, and immediate paradise are accepted as true religious premises, catastrophic violence can be internally rational, and religious believers may recognize that motivational logic particularly clearly.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris begins with an explicit concession and then explains, in a continuous response, why religious observers recognize the motivating beliefs.

components.text: Why religious observers may recognize Islamist totalitarian danger more readily.
Whether the asserted religious-versus-secular recognition frequency is empirically established.
Whether recognition of this threat demonstrates religion's broader comparative moral adequacy.

response.rationale: Harris justifies replacing the inference from recognition to religious moral superiority with an explanation based on familiarity with religious motivation, preserving the recognition issue while defeating its proposed consequence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, it explicitly explains the observed recognition while showing why that observation does not support the broader comparative inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The argument is expressly conditional on accepting martyrdom, jihad, and paradise premises, and its motivational conclusion is correspondingly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The strong claim is framed as internal rationality given specified beliefs, not as an unconditional endorsement or universal empirical claim.

charity.alternative: Religious Americans identify a real Islamist threat that secular academics may underestimate.
charity.decisiveQualification: Accurate threat recognition does not show that religion is the superior cause when religious premises also explain the threat's motivation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Given the stated afterlife and martyrdom premises, the inference to internally rational sacrificial violence is strong, with only empirical uptake left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move specifies the operative beliefs and motivational mechanism, but does not document their prevalence or compare rival political and social causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, it directly explains how religious premises can motivate violence and distort moral judgment.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris grants the recognition point and supplies a stronger competing explanation that directly limits its value for Prager's comparative conclusion.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris conditionally links beliefs in jihad, martyrdom, and immediate paradise to the internal rationality of dying in defense of faith.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: Whether religion has evidentiary support is distinct from the practical moral question of which worldview is more likely to produce a good society, a test on which anti-religious secular institutions allegedly failed by overlooking communism.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager interrupts to distinguish evidentiary questions from social consequences and then expressly states the comparative argument he is advancing.

components.text: Whether supernatural religious claims possess adequate evidentiary support.
Whether religion's practical record in recognizing evil should be evaluated separately.
Whether religious premises can make catastrophic violence internally rational.

response.rationale: Prager expressly separates evidentiary support from the practical social test and justifies attention to the latter, but this reframe does not answer Harris's causal account of religious violence.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within justified reframes, the replacement practical question is legitimate and explicit, though it preserves only part of the original challenge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between evidence and consequences is clear, but secular world, anti-religious secular world, and good world remain broad categories.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical verdict of moral failure from an asserted failure concerning communism lacks comparative scope conditions and supporting historical detail.

charity.alternative: A worldview may be evidentially unsupported even if some adherents identify particular social evils correctly.
charity.decisiveQualification: Practical success is relevant to comparative moral adequacy but cannot substitute for the creator-and-scripture evidentiary burden.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Separating truth evidence from practical consequences is sound, but one alleged institutional failure cannot by itself establish comparative worldview failure.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The communism example is asserted without specification, institutional comparison, or evidence that secularism rather than other factors explains the failure.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, the move expressly advances the proposed social-evil test for comparative worldview adequacy.

representationalCharity.rationale: Prager fairly distinguishes two questions, but his practical reframe risks sidelining rather than resolving the foundational evidentiary challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager distinguishes evidence for religion from which worldview makes a good society and cites secular failure to acknowledge communist evil.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Atheism was not the operative cause of communist, Nazi, or Khmer Rouge atrocities; closed political dogma was the common danger, while open-ended rational inquiry offers a general corrective to unjustified belief.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris rejects the proposed diagnosis, names political dogma as the relevant cause, and answers Prager's direct question about grounding the prohibition on murder.

components.text: Whether secular irreligion best explains failures involving communist and other totalitarian evils.
Whether religiosity generally makes people more likely to recognize grave totalitarian threats.
Whether open-ended rational inquiry supplies a corrective to dogmatic moral failure.

response.rationale: Harris expressly rejects atheism as the causal diagnosis, identifies closed political dogma as the operative common factor, and states open-ended rational inquiry as the defeating alternative.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly identifies the alleged causal error, substitutes a cross-case diagnosis, and states the consequence for the secular-failure inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal contrast is clear, although dogma across the board and rational people are broad terms whose institutional scope is only implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical rejection of atheism as the problem exceeds the excerpt's comparative evidence, though the common-dogma diagnosis is clearly articulated.

charity.alternative: Atheist regimes may have suppressed religious restraints and thereby contributed to totalitarian atrocities.
charity.decisiveQualification: The cited cases also involved coercive political dogmas, so atheism alone is not an adequate common-cause diagnosis.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The alternative common-cause diagnosis coherently defeats a simple atheism inference, with a bounded gap concerning whether atheism was contributory in some cases.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple totalitarian examples support the comparison, but the excerpt provides no detailed historical evidence disentangling political dogma from atheism.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, it directly advances open-ended rational inquiry as a corrective to unjustified political and religious belief.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris addresses the strongest causal interpretation by proposing a broader common factor, though he does not fully compare atheism's possible contributory role.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris rejects atheism as the best diagnosis of communist, Nazi, and Khmer Rouge evil and identifies closed political dogma instead.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The existence of persons capable of conversation, together with the existence and apparent design of the world, makes an intentional creator more plausible than treating human and cosmic existence as sheer coincidence.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager answers Harris's direct question about his belief and supplies a clearly personal, sustained inference from existence and design to a creator.

components.text: Whether sacred books were written or informed by a supernatural creator.
Whether there is any evidentiary basis for believing in an intentional creator.
Whether open-ended inquiry rather than dogma best corrects unjustified belief.

response.rationale: The design inference supplies issue-bearing support for a creator, but it does not contact the decisive claim that particular sacred books were supernaturally authored or informed.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it addresses an upstream creator question but not the decisive scripture-authorship demand selected as primary.

precisionFindings.rationale: The creator inference is clear and stable, though the intended comparison with coincidence implicitly excludes naturalistic mechanisms without defining them.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling unguided existence almost absurd asserts much more than the offered intuition supports and does not compare naturalistic alternatives.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic explanations need not treat persons or the world as sheer unexplained coincidence.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move must compare design with lawful natural processes, not merely with pure coincidence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is intelligible, but it presents an underdeveloped choice between intentional design and coincidence while omitting relevant naturalistic alternatives.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conclusion rests on asserted incredulity and apparent design without specific evidence, probability comparison, or engagement with rival explanations.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, it directly supplies a proposed basis for an intentional creator, though not for sacred teaching.

representationalCharity.rationale: Prager reduces the naturalistic alternative to coincidence and omits the decisive qualification that non-intentional explanations can invoke structured causal mechanisms.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager argues that persons, the world, creation, and apparent design are less plausibly coincidental than products of a creator or designer.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The prohibition on murder remains durable because it rests on divine authority, whereas reliance on discussion alone places unwarranted confidence in fallible human nature.
moves.attributionBasis: Prager explicitly contrasts his divine-command account with Harris's conversational account and states his judgment about their relative rationality.

components.text: Whether open-ended rational discussion can ground and preserve the prohibition on murder.
Whether political dogma rather than atheism best explains totalitarian atrocities.
Whether divine or religious premises can themselves rationalize lethal violence.

response.rationale: Prager directly contests the sufficiency of discussion and proposes divine authority as the durable basis of the anti-murder norm, while leaving the other causal challenges unanswered.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive grounding component but does not address challenges about conflicting religious commands or political causation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The divine-versus-discussion contrast is clear, but claims about what makes the norm prevail and about human nature lack temporal and institutional scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The causal claim that the norm prevails because God said it is asserted categorically without historical comparison or treatment of secular enforcement.

charity.alternative: Secular moral reasoning includes shared interests, empathy, institutions, and evidence, not merely casual neighborly discussion.
charity.decisiveQualification: Divine authority must show greater reliability despite disagreement over revelation and religiously sanctioned killing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Divine authority could provide a reason for obedience, but the move does not establish durability, resolve interpretive disagreement, or exclude secular grounds.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central historical and psychological claim is unsupported beyond assertion and a generalized distrust of fallible human nature.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, it directly addresses why divine authority allegedly makes a core prohibition binding and durable.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply substantially weakens the secular alternative to discussion and omits the decisive comparative problem of conflicting interpretations of divine commands.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager says the murder prohibition prevails because God commanded it and contrasts that authority with discussion and confidence in human nature.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Secular morality can ground concern in the happiness and suffering of conscious creatures and use differences in experiential and neurological capacity to distinguish the interests of humans, animals, embryos, and fetuses.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris answers Prager's challenge directly and repeatedly develops the same capacity-based account despite intervening questions and objections from Prager.

components.text: Whether secular morality has a substantive basis beyond divine command for protecting creatures from harm.
Whether human persons require an intentional creator to possess special moral significance.
Whether secular grounds make prohibitions as durable as divine authority allegedly does.

response.rationale: Harris supplies happiness, suffering, and conscious capacity as substantive secular grounds and applies them across life forms, but does not establish long-term durability of resulting rules.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive secular-grounding demand directly while leaving the comparative durability claim unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criterion is consistently framed in degrees of possible experience, and the move explicitly treats capacities as varying across creatures and developmental stages.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers capacity as a relevant basis and openly treats its degree in particular creatures as a question for further inquiry.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The link from capacity for happiness and suffering to moral concern is coherent, with one material normative bridge from morally relevant interests to obligations left implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The examples clarify how neurological and experiential differences matter, but no specific evidence establishes the capacities or resolves hard comparisons.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, it directly grounds moral distinctions in facts about conscious wellbeing, suffering, and experiential capacity.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move mainly develops a positive capacity-based account rather than relying on an interpretation of a specific opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris identifies happiness and suffering as morally relevant and asks what degrees of experience are possible in chickens, persons, embryos, and fetuses.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Faith-based certainty that a fully formed soul exists at conception polarizes abortion policy and obstructs nuanced discussion of ethically relevant differences across fetal development.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris identifies polarization as the explanation and attributes it specifically to conception-based soul dogma in a continuous answer to Prager's challenge.

components.text: Whether divine authority is necessary to make prohibitions against killing binding and durable.
Whether a supernatural account establishes human moral status from conception.
Whether religious dogma can impede good policy and practical moral judgment.

response.rationale: The abortion example attacks conception-based dogma and its policy effects but does not answer the primary comparative claim about divine authority making murder prohibitions durable.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within relevant nonanswers, it bears on religious authority and contested killing but does not contact the selected binding-obligation demand.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conception-soul mechanism is clear, but claims that secular people were forced into insensible discussion generalize broadly across participants and policy contexts.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical causal attribution of secular discourse failures to religious dogmatism lacks evidence and omits other sources of polarization.

charity.alternative: Conception-based moral status may be defended philosophically rather than accepted solely as faith-based soul dogma.
charity.decisiveQualification: The criticism applies most directly to certainty resting on revelation, not to every argument for conception-based protection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Absolute conception certainty can obstruct developmental distinctions, but the move overstates its causal responsibility for the quality of all secular policy discussion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The claimed polarizing mechanism is plausible but supported only by assertion, without policy examples or comparison with nonreligious causes.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within subsidiary support, it directly shows how secular developmental distinctions may be obstructed by conception-based dogma.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris identifies a real dogmatic form of the position but treats it too broadly and omits the strongest non-revelatory alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris attributes polarized abortion discourse to dogmatic certainty that a fully formed soul exists at conception and suppresses developmental distinctions.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Ethical realism differs from pragmatism because moral questions can have right and wrong answers grounded in the possible happiness and suffering of conscious physical systems.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris expressly corrects Prager's characterization of realism, defines his own position, and applies it to failures by both secular activists and religious believers.

components.text: Whether Harris's secular account is merely pragmatic rather than realist and truth-apt.
Whether secular moral discussion can yield right and wrong answers rather than preference.
Whether a creator is required to ground the moral status of conscious physical systems.

response.rationale: Harris expressly identifies the pragmatism characterization as mistaken, defines realism through right and wrong answers, and states conscious wellbeing as the proposed truth-grounding domain.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it directly corrects the category error and supplies the consequential replacement account needed to preserve the moral-knowledge issue.

precisionFindings.rationale: Realism is explicitly contrasted with pragmatism, and the proposed domain is consistently limited to systems capable of happiness and suffering.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The account clearly asserts objective answers but does not fully warrant how facts about possible experience generate unique moral truths.

charity.alternative: A wellbeing account may still be pragmatic if it values outcomes without establishing stance-independent moral truth.
charity.decisiveQualification: Asserting right and wrong answers distinguishes the intention of realism, but an ontological and epistemic bridge is still required.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction from pragmatism is coherent, but the inference from factual possibilities of happiness and suffering to objective moral answers leaves a material bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The conscious-system criterion supplies a substantive basis, but the excerpt does not demonstrate how competing welfare measures yield determinate answers.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within motion-tier support, it directly claims that secular realism can supply objective moral answers grounded in conscious wellbeing.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris fairly corrects the label and states a realist thesis, while the strongest objection remains that the truth-making bridge is compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris explicitly opposes realism to pragmatism and grounds right and wrong answers in happiness and suffering possible for conscious physical systems.

moves.speaker: Dennis Prager
moves.proposition: The Bible's exceptional moral character supports its divine authorship, and rules that appear primitive in isolation can constitute major moral advances when interpreted within their historical setting.
moves.attributionBasis: The opening row contains the end of Harris's question and the beginning of Prager's answer, after which Prager develops the scriptural argument through the final row.

components.text: Whether scripture's moral character supplies evidence of supernatural or divine authorship.
Whether scriptural injunctions are dangerous or morally defective when read as authoritative.
Whether open-ended inquiry is superior to dogmatic authority as a corrective mechanism.
Whether conscious capacity rather than scripture grounds contested moral distinctions.

response.rationale: Prager directly offers scripture's alleged moral character and historical progress as answers to the unsupported and morally defective scripture challenges, while leaving secular-grounding alternatives untouched.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive scripture-credibility component but supplies only one compressed historical illustration and no authorship bridge.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical-progress defense is recoverable, but the excerpt incompletely presents the divine-authorship claim and shifts between one rule and scripture's overall character.

calibrationFindings.rationale: A sweeping inference from exceptional moral character to divine authorship is not warranted by the single compressed eye-for-an-eye example.

charity.alternative: Biblical rules can represent local historical advances while remaining human, morally mixed, and unsuitable as timeless commands.
charity.decisiveQualification: Relative improvement in an ancient setting does not establish divine authorship or timeless moral reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Historical context can answer charges of primitiveness, but the move does not bridge relative moral advance to exceptional overall character or divine authorship.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt offers one undeveloped example and an appeal to the speaker's years of study rather than representative textual or historical support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central support, it directly attempts to establish sacred teaching's moral credibility and infer divine authorship.

representationalCharity.rationale: Prager usefully invokes historical context but does not address the strongest alternative that genuine progress can occur in a wholly human and mixed text.

moves.evidenceBasis: Prager offers to explain disputed injunctions historically and cites eye for an eye as a rule commonly called primitive but allegedly representing major advancement.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: Given human attachment, the value placed on cooperation, and the psychological benefits of love and mutual care, societies have secular grounds to reject murder without relying on divine command.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris answers Prager's hypothetical about a person endorsing murder and gives a continuous social and psychological account of why that position fails.

components.text: Whether secular human nature and social reasoning can ground rejection of murder without divine command.
Whether the secular prohibition remains as durable as one based on divine authority.
Whether secular social arrangements can contribute to a good and viable society.

response.rationale: Harris directly supplies attachment, cooperation, and psychological benefits as secular grounds against murder, but does not fully answer the comparative durability challenge.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within partial answers, it contacts the decisive grounding demand explicitly while leaving the historical durability comparison substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cooperation-based mechanism is clear and consistently social, though exceptional individuals or societies that reject reciprocity are handled only implicitly.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The claim is framed as a likely social consequence for a murder-endorsing person, and ordinary human attachment plausibly supports that limited force.

charity.alternative: Divine command may motivate obedience even when immediate cooperative incentives fail.
charity.decisiveQualification: That motivational advantage would not show divine command is necessary, especially where attachment, institutions, and reciprocity independently constrain killing.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The social mechanism coherently explains broad rejection of murder, with one bounded gap between social unviability and an objective binding prohibition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The account invokes familiar human attachments and cooperative incentives but provides no specific psychological or historical evidence for their sufficiency.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within subsidiary support, it directly explains how attachment, reciprocity, care, and viable cooperation sustain an anti-murder norm.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses the necessity claim with a genuine secular mechanism while leaving unusual cases of weak cooperative incentives underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris invokes human nature, the primacy of cooperation, love, nurturance, and the social isolation or danger facing a person who endorses murder.

moves.speaker: Sam Harris
moves.proposition: The legal worldview found across Leviticus and Deuteronomy is violently theocratic rather than a dependable timeless moral guide, and later moral progress required societies to outgrow it.
moves.attributionBasis: Harris invites listeners to examine the named biblical legal books and draws an explicit comparative conclusion about their governing worldview and later rejection.

components.text: Whether historical context vindicates biblical law as exceptional moral progress and evidence of divine authorship.
Whether Leviticus and Deuteronomy provide a dependable timeless governing morality.
Whether divine-command authority reliably prohibits killing rather than licensing it.
Whether religion's historical record supports its comparative capacity to make a good society.

response.rationale: Harris identifies pervasive theocratic killing as the feature defeating the claim of exceptional scriptural morality and states that later societies achieved progress by outgrowing that worldview.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within diagnostic defeats, it explicitly targets the scripture-character inference, names contrary textual content, and states the defeating historical consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The theocracy objection is clear, but the claim that killing never stops is rhetorical and the move generalizes from named legal books to a broader biblical worldview.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The comparison with Taliban theocracy and pervasive killing is categorical, while the excerpt supplies no passages, proportions, or historical qualifications.

charity.alternative: Some harsh biblical laws may have limited retaliation or represented improvements relative to neighboring ancient practices.
charity.decisiveQualification: Local relative advances can coexist with a coercive theocratic legal system and do not establish timeless or divine moral reliability.

logicalCoherence.rationale: If the named legal corpus pervasively mandates theocratic violence, later rejection strongly challenges timeless reliability, though the comparative textual premise remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Naming Leviticus and Deuteronomy makes the challenge inspectable, but no representative passages or contextual comparison substantiate the sweeping characterization.

relevanceBurden.rationale: Within central attack, it directly challenges scripture's moral credibility and therefore the creator-and-scripture authority bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: Harris's broader textual challenge preserves the possibility of local advances while directly contesting the inference to dependable overall moral authority.

moves.evidenceBasis: Harris directs listeners to Leviticus and Deuteronomy, characterizes their legal worldview as intensely theocratic and violent, and says society outgrew it.

pro.rationale: No distinct pro-side debate-wide burden consequence remains outside the move ratings, response links, relevance judgments, and importance assignments.

eligibility.completionCriterion: No uncaptured completion criterion was identified.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No distinct residual consequence was identified.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the proposed residual would not change any burden-completion determination.

con.rationale: No distinct con-side debate-wide burden consequence remains outside the move ratings, response links, relevance judgments, and importance assignments.

eligibility.completionCriterion: No uncaptured completion criterion was identified.
eligibility.distinctConsequence: No distinct residual consequence was identified.
eligibility.counterfactual: Removing the proposed residual would not change any burden-completion determination.
